title: Long-distance relationships: 7 habits to feel closer every day
description: Seven practical ideas for a long-distance relationship: rituals, questions, shared moments and planning reunions, without pressure.
summary: To feel closer at a distance, choose a realistic small ritual, share ordinary moments and plan your next reunion together. Regular contact should remain an invitation: everyone can need time to themselves.

sections.title: 1. Find a rhythm that works for both of you
paragraphs: An internship abroad, studying in different cities or mismatched schedules can change when you connect. Start by explaining when you are available instead of expecting an immediate reply.
Try a ten-minute catch-up two or three evenings a week. After a week, adjust: does it feel enjoyable or like another obligation? A helpful habit leaves room for unexpected changes.

sections.title: 2. Replace an automatic question with real curiosity
paragraphs: ‘How are you?’ is sometimes enough, but may not open much conversation. Try ‘Which moment today would you have liked to share with me?’ Answer it yourself too, and listen without immediately trying to solve a problem.

sections.title: 3. Share something ordinary
paragraphs: A photo of lunch, a song from your bus ride or a small win at work gives you something to talk about beyond big updates. Pick a detail you want to share without turning your day into a report.

sections.title: 4. Plan a date at a distance
paragraphs: Cook the same recipe, watch an episode together or play a short game. Agree on a start time and approximate length. Afterwards, ask what you would like to do again: a good activity is one you both enjoy.

sections.title: 5. Make your next reunion tangible
paragraphs: Where possible, note the next visit date and choose something simple to do together. If your budget or schedule gets in the way, agree when to revisit the plan. A countdown can make waiting enjoyable without promising something you cannot deliver.

sections.title: 6. Keep a space for your memories
paragraphs: Gather a few moments in a shared album with a sentence about what they mean. When conversation runs dry, choose a memory and say what you would like to experience again. Ask before sharing an image outside your space.

sections.title: 7. Leave room for a pause
paragraphs: A late reply alone does not explain how your partner feels. Agree on a simple way to say ‘Busy day, I’ll catch up tomorrow.’ Questions, location sharing and activities should remain choices, never proof someone has to provide.

Nearly is designed to bring questions, moods, memories, a calendar and a reunion countdown into a private couple space. The app is coming soon to iOS and Android; you can already try couple questions on the website without an account.

faqs.question: Do long-distance couples need to talk every day?
faqs.answer: There is no single right frequency. Agree on a rhythm that fits your schedules and adjust if either person feels overlooked or pressured.

faqs.question: What can we do when we run out of conversation topics?
faqs.answer: Start with a memory, try an open question or suggest a short activity such as cooking the same recipe. A call can also feel good without constant conversation.

title: Couple questions: a five-minute ritual you will want to keep
description: A simple ritual and ten couple questions to move beyond ‘How are you?’, listen and share a moment, far apart or under the same roof.
summary: A couple ritual can take five minutes: one open question, an answer from each person and a small gesture afterwards. Choose a calm moment and always leave room to skip a question.

sections.title: A simple format to try tonight
paragraphs: Choose a question before you start. One person answers and the other listens, then swap. Finish by naming something you appreciated about the exchange. The aim is to discover a detail, not complete a list.
Try it out loud, on a walk or in writing if your schedules differ. Avoid a sensitive question when someone has to leave. If five minutes is not enough, suggest returning to it later.

sections.title: 10 questions to start without pressure
paragraphs: Choose according to your mood: not every conversation needs to be deep. A light question can be a good start after a long day.
bullets: What little moment would you like us to share this week?
Which song reminds you of us?
Which memory of us would you describe as a film scene?
What are you proud of at the moment?
What small gesture would make you happy this week?
What would you like to learn with me?
What would our ideal Sunday look like?
When do you feel most listened to?
What small adventure could we plan together?

sections.title: Listen before responding
paragraphs: An answer unlike yours is not a bad result. Ask ‘Would you like to tell me more?’ instead of comparing straight away. If your partner describes a difficulty, ask whether they want an idea or just someone to listen.
Agree that either person can skip a question. Avoid saving an answer to use as an argument later: the ritual works better when the exchange feels trustworthy.

faqs.answer: Choose questions about daily life, memories or the next reunion. ‘Which moment would you have liked to share with me?’ is a simple starting point.

title: Stay connected with friends and family when you live far apart
description: Easy ideas to stay close to friends and family at a distance: updates, private memories, games and relaxed catch-ups.
summary: To stay connected with loved ones, alternate small updates, memories and realistic catch-ups. A shared space helps you find those moments again; what matters is choosing habits everyone can access.

sections.title: Give updates a starting point
paragraphs: After a move, a group chat can fall silent without the friendships becoming less important. Suggest a relaxed habit: a Sunday photo or one good thing from the week. Explain that taking part is optional.

With family, choose a format that works for those less familiar with apps. A photo with one sentence can provide more context than a stream of pictures. Individual calls still have a place alongside the group.

sections.title: Do something together, even briefly
paragraphs: With friends, a quiz, a photo challenge or a short game can restart the conversation. With family, tell the story of an object, share a recipe or ask about a favourite holiday memory.
Offer a window rather than demanding an instant response: everyone could contribute over the weekend. For live games, confirm the time zone and duration so nobody has to miss sleep.

sections.title: Keep memories in the right circle
paragraphs: A group album is easier to revisit than a photo buried in a conversation. Add a date, place or anecdote. Before inviting a new member or reposting a photo, ask the people concerned.
Keep family memories and your friends’ moments separate: the circles may not want to share the same things. Nearly is designed around distinct relationship spaces accessible to invited members.

sections.title: Turn ‘We should meet up’ into a next step
paragraphs: Suggest two dates and a simple activity instead of waiting for the perfect weekend. If meeting is impossible, choose the next call or a remote game night. A modest, achievable date can be more useful than a big plan that never happens.

Nearly’s concept brings together friends and family spaces, questions, moments, games and a calendar. The app is announced for iOS and Android; the website’s game quiz already helps you discover an activity for your group.

faqs.question: How can I reconnect with a friend after months without contact?
faqs.answer: Send a simple message with a specific memory and an invitation that is easy to decline or reschedule. You can acknowledge the time apart without asking them to justify their silence.

faqs.question: Is Nearly only for couples?
faqs.answer: No. Nearly is designed for couples, friends and families, with a distinct private space for each connection.

title: A night with friends: games, photos and shared expenses made simple
description: Plan a night with friends in four steps: choose a game, keep photos private and work out who owes whom with a practical example.
summary: An easier evening starts with an agreed budget and an activity that suits the group. Keep photos in a chosen circle and record expenses as you go so repayments are clear.

sections.title: Before the evening: agree on the basics
paragraphs: Confirm the place, time and approximate budget. Decide whether groceries are shared by everyone or just those using them. Agreeing before a purchase avoids charging someone for an expense they did not expect.
Plan an appropriate journey home for everyone and offer alcohol-free drinks. A good evening does not require drinking or joining every game.

sections.title: Choose a game everyone can join
paragraphs: Start with a short activity and explain the rules in a minute. A group quiz or light questions can include people who know one another less well. Allow people to pass and avoid challenges that expose private information.
Nearly’s game quiz suggests an activity based on your answers. It can help you prepare; the app’s adult-only Party Mode is still coming soon.

sections.title: Decide where the photos go
paragraphs: Ask before photographing, then before publishing. Share the album only with the agreed people and accept requests to remove a picture. A private space does not replace consent.
Nearly plans a locked photo vault in Party. You can explore its presentation on the site, but do not assume that a tool makes every possible copy of an image impossible.

sections.title: Split the expenses: an example with three people
paragraphs: Alice pays €60 for groceries, Bilal pays €30 for pizza and Chloé pays nothing upfront. If the €90 is shared equally, each person owes €30. Alice has paid €30 too much, Bilal is even and Chloé owes €30: Chloé repays Alice.

Record expenses before you forget who paid and check the participants for each purchase. Nearly’s calculator is available without an account for a trial limited to three expenses. It calculates repayments; it does not make bank transfers.

faqs.question: How do you split expenses for an evening with friends?
faqs.answer: Add up shared expenses, define each person’s share and subtract what they have already paid. If a purchase concerns only part of the group, divide it among those participants.

faqs.question: Does the Nearly calculator send money?
faqs.answer: No. It shows who owes whom. You arrange the payment separately with the people involved.

Invite a small group first and check that everyone can find an update, respond and understand who can see what. Ease of use for your loved ones matters more than a long feature list.
